n: Basilica of Our Lady of Zapopan
w: A 17th-century Franciscan sanctuary built around a wooden Virgin that crossed the Atlantic from Spain in the 1500s -- one of Western Mexico's most visited pilgrimage sites. The complex also quietly houses the Huichol Museum, dedicated to the region's Indigenous culture.
s: Home to a centuries-old Virgin revered across Mexico
_facts: 17th-century Franciscan sanctuary in downtown Zapopan
One of the most visited sanctuaries in Western Mexico
Preserves a wooden Virgin of medieval origin brought from Spain in the 16th century
Huichol Museum is located in the building

w: A bronze goddess of wisdom, given deliberately Indigenous facial features and set spinning atop a roundabout fountain, her pedestal naming eighteen notable citizens beneath the motto 'may justice, wisdom and strength guard this loyal city.' Once mocked by residents, she is now Guadalajara's emblem.
s: A goddess with an Indigenous face, now the city's symbol
_facts: Statue of Minerva in a roundabout fountain, known as La Minerva
Pedestal inscribed with names of 18 notable citizens
Depicted with Indigenous facial features, holding spear and shield
Initially criticized, later became a symbol of the city

w: Clad in white marble quarried in Torreon and topped with a spire bearing the angel Moroni, this was the 11th Latter-day Saint temple built in Mexico. Church president Gordon B. Hinckley dedicated it in 2001, two years after ground was broken in Zapopan.
s: A gleaming Mormon temple with marble from Torreon
_facts: Temple of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Zapopan
11th LDS temple built in Mexico, 105th operating worldwide
71 feet tall, white marble exterior from Torreon
Groundbreaking June 1999; dedicated by Gordon B. Hinckley, 29 April 2001

w: An indoor amphitheatre built as the centerpiece of the University of Guadalajara's cultural complex, designed by architect Jose de Arimatea Moyao and bankrolled by the telecom giant whose name it carries. Considered the main show venue for the whole of Western Mexico.
_facts: Indoor amphitheatre in Zapopan, sponsored by Telmex
Centerpiece of the University Cultural Center project, University of Guadalajara
Designed by architect Jose de Arimatea Moyao
Considered the main show center in Western Mexico

w: Closed to new burials since 1896 but very much open to visitors, this 19th-century cemetery has built a reputation on its legends -- ghost stories dense enough to support regular night tours alongside the daytime ones. Guadalajara's most atmospheric graveyard.
s: A 19th-century cemetery famous for its ghost tours
_facts: Historic cemetery also known as Santa Paula Cemetery
Opened 1848, formally closed for burials 1896
Site of legends and night tours, still open for daytime and evening visits

w: Better known by its market name than its official one, Mercado Libertad claims the title of largest indoor market in all of Latin America -- 40,000 square metres of stalls under one roof. A sensory overload of a shopping trip, Guadalajara-style.
_facts: Officially Mercado Libertad, popularly San Juan de Dios Market
Largest indoor market in Latin America
Area of 40,000 square metres
